essays.stem: Describe a tensile test: the test piece, what is measured, and what the yield strength, ultimate tensile strength and elongation tell a fabricator.
essays.modelAnswer: A tensile test piece is machined from the material or from a welded joint to a set shape, with a marked gauge length and a known cross-sectional area. It is gripped in a testing machine and pulled slowly until it breaks, while the load and the stretch are recorded. Stress is the load divided by the area, in N/mm². At first the piece stretches elastically and would spring back. The yield strength is the stress at which it starts to stretch permanently; designers keep working stresses below this, so a structure does not bend out of shape. The ultimate tensile strength is the highest stress it takes before it necks and breaks. The elongation is the increase in gauge length after breaking, given as a percentage; a high elongation shows a ductile metal that will bend and give warning before failing. A fabricator uses these figures, from the mill certificate or the welding procedure test, to check that the material and the welds are strong and ductile enough.
markingPoints: Describes the test piece and the machine pulling it to failure
Stress = load ÷ area; elastic stretch before yield
Yield strength: start of permanent stretch; design stays below it
UTS: highest stress before failure
Elongation as a percentage shows ductility; links to certificates or weld tests

essays.stem: Explain hardness tests (Brinell, Vickers and Rockwell) and the Charpy impact test, and say when each would be useful to a welding fabricator.
essays.modelAnswer: Hardness tests press a hard indenter into the surface with a set load. The Brinell test uses a hardened ball and measures the width of the dent; it suits softer metals and rough parts such as plate and castings. The Vickers test uses a square-based diamond pyramid and measures the diagonals of the mark; it can be used on very small areas, so it is used to check the hardness of weld metal and the heat-affected zone in a cut and polished weld section. The Rockwell test measures the depth of the indent and gives a quick reading on a dial, so it suits checking parts on the shop floor, such as hardened tools. A fabricator uses hardness results to check that a weld or HAZ has not become too hard and brittle. The Charpy test strikes a small notched bar with a swinging pendulum and measures the energy absorbed in joules. It shows toughness, and is used for steels and welds that must not break suddenly, especially at low temperatures, such as in pressure vessels and structures.
markingPoints: Hardness tests press an indenter into the surface
Brinell: ball, suits plate and castings
Vickers: diamond pyramid, small areas such as weld and HAZ
Rockwell: depth reading, quick shop-floor checks
Charpy: notched bar, pendulum, energy in joules, toughness for welds and cold service

essays.stem: Explain what the carbon equivalent (CE) of a steel is and how it affects weldability. Say what a welder can do when welding a steel with a high carbon equivalent.
essays.modelAnswer: The carbon equivalent is a single number worked out from a steel's chemical analysis, usually found on the mill certificate. Carbon has the strongest effect on how hard steel gets when it cools quickly, and other alloying elements such as manganese, chromium, molybdenum, nickel and copper also add to it, so the formula adds a share of each to the carbon content. The higher the CE, the harder and more brittle the heat-affected zone can become as the weld cools, and the greater the risk of hydrogen (cold) cracking. A low CE steel, such as most mild steels, is easy to weld. For a steel with a high CE, the welder should follow the welding procedure, which may call for preheat and a set interpass temperature to slow the cooling. They should use low-hydrogen electrodes or processes, with consumables kept dry as the maker says, and clean the joint of rust, oil and moisture. A higher heat input, slow cooling after welding and sometimes post-weld heat treatment may also be used.
markingPoints: CE is worked out from the steel's chemistry (carbon plus other elements)
Higher CE means a harder HAZ and more risk of cracking
Low-CE steels such as mild steel weld easily
Controls: follow the procedure, preheat and interpass temperature
Low-hydrogen consumables, dry and clean, controlled cooling or heat treatment

essays.stem: Compare austenitic, ferritic and martensitic stainless steels. Cover magnetism, hardening, corrosion resistance, typical uses and points to watch when welding.
essays.modelAnswer: All stainless steels contain at least about 10.5% chromium, which forms a thin protective oxide film. Austenitic stainless, such as 304 and 316, also contains nickel. It is non-magnetic when annealed, cannot be hardened by heat treatment, only by cold work, and has the best general corrosion resistance. It is used for food equipment, handrails and tanks. It welds well, but it expands a lot and conducts heat poorly, so it distorts, and low-carbon 'L' grades are used to protect corrosion resistance near the weld. Ferritic stainless, such as 430, is magnetic, cannot be hardened by heat treatment, is cheaper and has fair corrosion resistance; it is used for trims and exhaust parts. Its grain can grow when welded, which makes it less tough. Martensitic stainless, such as 410 or 420, is magnetic and can be hardened and tempered. It is used for knives, tools and shafts. It has lower corrosion resistance and can crack when welded, so it needs preheat and heat treatment after welding.
markingPoints: All contain chromium (about 10.5% or more) forming a protective film
Austenitic: nickel, non-magnetic, not heat-hardenable, best corrosion resistance, food and rails
Ferritic: magnetic, not heat-hardenable, cheaper, trims
Martensitic: magnetic, hardenable, knives and tools
Welding points for each (distortion, L grades, grain growth, preheat and PWHT)

essays.stem: Explain how and why aluminium alloys behave differently from steel when they are cut and welded.
essays.modelAnswer: Aluminium is about one third of the weight of steel. Its surface oxide film melts at about 2000 °C, far hotter than the aluminium itself at about 660 °C, so it must be removed with a stainless steel brush or by the cleaning action of the arc just before welding, or it causes lack of fusion. Aluminium conducts heat several times better than steel, so the heat flows away fast and more heat input, or preheat on thick sections, is needed. It expands about twice as much as steel, so it distorts more and needs good clamping, tacking and welding sequence. It does not change colour before it melts, so the welder must watch the weld pool closely. Hydrogen from damp, grease or dirty filler causes porosity, so everything must be clean and dry. Heat-treatable alloys lose some strength in the heat-affected zone. Aluminium is not magnetic and does not give sparks when cut. It is soft and clogs abrasive discs and saw blades, so the right blades and discs are kept for aluminium only.
markingPoints: Oxide film melts far above aluminium: must be removed
High heat conductivity: more heat input or preheat
High expansion: more distortion, needs control
No colour change before melting; porosity from hydrogen and dirt
Strength loss in heat-treated alloys; separate discs and blades

essays.stem: Explain galvanic corrosion, using an example from a coastal job in Jamaica, and describe how to design and fabricate to prevent it.
essays.modelAnswer: Galvanic corrosion happens when two different metals touch each other and are both wet with an electrolyte, such as salty rain or sea spray. The two metals act like a battery: the less noble metal (the anode) corrodes faster, and the more noble metal (the cathode) is protected. For example, on a beach bar in Negril, stainless steel screws holding aluminium roof sheet or an aluminium sign bracket will cause the aluminium around them to corrode, and bare mild steel bolted to copper or stainless will rust quickly. The effect is worse when the less noble metal has a small area compared with the noble one. To prevent it, choose metals close together in the galvanic series, or the same metal for fasteners and parts. Separate different metals with insulating washers, sleeves, gaskets or a sealant. Paint or coat both metals, especially the more noble one. Design joints so water drains away and does not sit in crevices. Where suitable, use zinc as a sacrificial coating or anode, as in galvanising.
markingPoints: Two different metals in contact with an electrolyte
The less noble metal (anode) corrodes; the noble one is protected
Gives a correct coastal Jamaican example
Mentions area effect or the galvanic series in choosing metals
Prevention: insulation, coatings, drainage, sacrificial zinc

essays.stem: Explain annealing, normalising, hardening and tempering, and stress relieving: how each is done, why, and where a fabricator might meet each one.
essays.modelAnswer: Annealing heats steel to its hardening range, holds it, then cools it very slowly, often in the furnace. It makes the steel as soft and ductile as possible, for example before heavy bending or after cold work. Normalising heats steel to a similar temperature and lets it cool in still air. It gives a finer, more even grain, and is used on forgings, hot-formed parts and some plate. Hardening heats a medium- or high-carbon steel to red heat and quenches it in water or oil, which makes it very hard but brittle. Tempering then reheats the hardened steel to a lower temperature to take away some brittleness and make it tougher. A fabricator meets these when making or dressing chisels, punches and tools. Stress relieving heats a welded part to a temperature below the hardening range, holds it, then cools it slowly. It lowers the stresses locked in by welding, which reduces distortion when the part is later machined and lowers the risk of cracking. It is used on thick welded frames and pressure parts, as the procedure says.
markingPoints: Annealing: heat, slow cool in furnace; softest; before bending or after cold work
Normalising: heat, cool in still air; refines grain
Hardening: heat and quench; hard but brittle
Tempering: reheat to a lower temperature; tougher; tools
Stress relieving: below hardening range, slow cool; reduces weld stresses

essays.stem: Explain how materials are traced in a fabrication shop from delivery to the finished job, and why traceability matters.
essays.modelAnswer: When steel is delivered, the store checks it against the purchase order and the delivery note for grade, size and quantity, and checks that the mill test certificates have come with it. The heat number stamped or painted on each plate or bar is matched to its certificate, and the material is booked into a register and stored on a marked rack, with any unmarked or doubtful material kept apart until it is confirmed. When material is cut, the heat number and grade are copied onto each part, often by hard stamp or paint marker, before the offcut is returned to stock with its own mark. The cutting list or job card records which heat number each part came from. Welding consumables are recorded in the same way by batch. At the end, the records and certificates go into the job file. Traceability matters because if a fault, crack or failure is found, the source can be found, other parts made from the same batch can be checked, and the client and inspector can see that the right materials were used.
markingPoints: Checks delivery against order, with certificates
Matches heat numbers to certificates; registers and racks stock; quarantines doubtful material
Transfers heat number and grade to cut parts and offcuts
Records on cutting lists or job cards, including consumable batches; job file
Why: find the cause of faults, check other parts, prove the right material

essays.stem: A frame is made from 6 lengths of 50 × 50 × 5 mm steel angle, each 2.4 m long, and two plates 1 m × 0.5 m × 6 mm. Work out its approximate mass, showing your working, and explain why such calculations matter.
essays.modelAnswer: Take the density of steel as 7850 kg/m³. For the angle, the cross-section is about (50 + 45) × 5 = 475 mm², which is 0.000475 m². One metre weighs 0.000475 × 7850 = about 3.7 kg; tables give about 3.8 kg per metre because of the rounded corners. The total length is 6 × 2.4 = 14.4 m, so the angle weighs about 14.4 × 3.7 = about 54 kg. For each plate, the volume is 1 × 0.5 × 0.006 = 0.003 m³, so the mass is 0.003 × 7850 = 23.55 kg, and two plates are about 47 kg. The frame is about 54 + 47 = about 101 kg, plus the weld metal. These calculations matter because they tell us how to lift and move the frame safely, whether a team lift is enough or a hoist is needed, and how to rate slings. They are also used to cost and order the steel, since steel is often priced by mass, and to work out transport loads.
markingPoints: Uses density 7850 kg/m³ and converts mm to m correctly
Angle: about 3.7–3.8 kg/m, about 54 kg for 14.4 m
Plates: 23.55 kg each, about 47 kg for two
Total about 100 kg
Why: safe lifting and slinging, costing and ordering, transport

essays.stem: As team leader, explain how you would choose and justify the material for a staircase at a beach-front hotel, weighing strength, corrosion, weldability, cost, availability and maintenance.
essays.modelAnswer: I start with what the staircase must do: carry people safely, last many years in salty sea air, look good and be maintained by the hotel. For strength, mild steel, stainless steel and aluminium alloys can all be designed to carry the load, but aluminium needs larger sections. For corrosion, plain mild steel rusts fast near the sea unless it is hot-dip galvanised and painted, and the coating must be kept up. Grade 316 stainless steel resists salt spray well, and aluminium resists it if fasteners are chosen to avoid galvanic corrosion. For weldability, mild steel is easiest; stainless needs care with distortion and cleaning; aluminium needs TIG or MIG skills and loses strength near the weld. For cost, galvanised mild steel is cheapest to make, stainless costs the most, and aluminium is in between. I check what is available locally and how quickly. For maintenance, stainless needs only washing, while painted steel needs repainting. I would recommend a galvanised and painted mild steel structure with 316 stainless handrails, and write the reasons and costs down for the client and supervisor.
markingPoints: States the job's needs (load, sea air, appearance, maintenance)
Compares strength and corrosion of the options correctly
Compares weldability and fabrication needs
Considers cost, availability and maintenance
Makes a clear recommendation and records the reasons

practical1.title: Heat treat and test carbon steel samples, and write a test report
practical1.brief: As a team, plan and carry out heat treatments on four labelled samples of the same medium- or high-carbon steel bar that the assessor gives you (about 10–12 mm diameter or square, 150 mm long), plus one sample left as supplied. Before you start, write a short test plan: the treatments, the order, who does each step, the hazards and the controls. Anneal one sample (heat to red and cool slowly in dry sand or ash), normalise one (heat to red and cool in still air), harden one (heat to red and quench in water or oil, as the assessor directs), and harden and then temper one (polish a strip and reheat gently until a straw to brown colour shows, then cool). Test every sample, including the one as supplied, with a file test and a bend test in the vice with a length of tube, and note how each one files, bends or breaks. Record the results in a table and write a one-page test report that explains the results. Each member carries out at least one treatment and one test while the assessor watches, and every member writes part of the report. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the report is finished and the area is clean.
materials: Five samples of medium- or high-carbon steel bar, each about 150 mm long, labelled 1 to 5
Oxy-fuel heating torch or a small forge, with a fire brick hearth
Quench tank of water (or oil, if the Centre allows), dry sand or ash, tongs
Emery cloth, files, bench vice and a length of steel tube
Test plan and results sheet, report paper
photos: The written test plan and the labelled samples
A sample being heated to red, with PPE worn
Quenching, with the member standing to one side of the tank
The tempering colours on the polished strip
The file test and bend test on each sample
All five tested samples laid out with the results table and the report
checklist: Helped write the test plan, including the hazards and controls
Set up and used the heating equipment safely, following the Centre's rules
Carried out their treatment correctly (heat, cooling method, timing)
Tested samples correctly and recorded what they found
Kept every sample labelled so the results could be traced
Explained the results correctly in their part of the report (soft, hard, brittle, tough)
Wore the right PPE and handled hot metal only with tongs
Left the area safe, with hot samples marked and the equipment shut down
safety: Follow the Centre's hot work rules; check the gas equipment and keep an extinguisher at hand
Wear a face shield or safety glasses, heat-resistant gloves, leather apron and safety boots
Quench by lowering the sample in with tongs, standing to one side; never use oil unless the assessor allows it, and keep a lid at hand
Treat all samples as hot; mark them and leave them on the hearth to cool
Wear safety glasses for the bend test; hardened samples can snap and fly
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Receive, identify and control a mixed delivery of materials, and write a material schedule for a job
practical2.brief: As a team, act as the Centre's materials team. The assessor gives you a mixed 'delivery' of stock (for example mild steel flat and angle, galvanised tube, stainless steel sheet and bar, aluminium plate, brass or copper pieces and some plastics), a purchase order, a delivery note and copies of mill certificates. First, plan how you will check the delivery and who does what. Check each item against the order and the delivery note, and match heat numbers to certificates. Identify every item using markings, a magnet, appearance and weight, and keep any item that cannot be confirmed apart with a 'quarantine' label. Measure each item, work out its mass, label it with grade, size and heat number, and store it on the right rack, with stainless and aluminium kept apart from carbon steel. Update a material register. Then use the stock to write a material schedule for a small job the assessor names (for example a coastal handrail): the material chosen for each part, the reasons, the sizes, quantities and masses. Each member checks and labels part of the delivery, and every member writes part of the schedule. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the register and schedule are finished and the store is tidy.
materials: A mixed set of stock items with some markings removed (from the assessor)
Purchase order, delivery note and copies of mill certificates
Magnet, steel tape, vernier caliper, scales if available
Material register sheet, calculator and schedule sheet
photos: The plan for checking the delivery
Items being checked against the delivery note and certificates
A member identifying an item with a magnet and markings
Labelled items stored on the correct racks, with the quarantine items apart
The finished material schedule for the job
checklist: Checked items against the order, delivery note and certificates
Identified materials correctly and used safe, suitable methods
Quarantined any item that could not be confirmed
Measured items and worked out masses correctly
Labelled and stored items correctly, keeping stainless and aluminium apart
Wrote clear, accurate entries in the register and schedule
Gave sound reasons for the materials chosen in the schedule
Handled materials safely and left the store tidy
safety: Wear gloves and safety boots; sheet and bar ends are sharp
Use team lifts or lifting aids for heavy or long items; plan each lift
Store long items securely on racks so they cannot roll or fall
Read the SDS for any coated or plastic material before cutting or heating
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
